1:
Gill states the object in a word — the thing to be done to Aaron and his sons is to hallow them, to sanctify, set apart and consecrate. Ellicott sets out the shape of the whole rite before any of it begins. The consecration had been commanded in the previous chapter; here the method is laid down, and it consists of five things — ablution, investiture, anointing, sacrifice, and the filling of the hand. All of them he takes as symbolical acts typical of things spiritual: washing of the putting away of impurity, robing of being clothed with holiness, unction of the giving of divine grace, so that the whole forms an acted parable, full of instruction to anyone who understood its meaning. Clarke gives the same sequence as a table of contents, and enters one chronological caution: the consecration did not actually take place until after the tabernacle had been erected.

Henry reads the elaborateness as deliberate on two sides. The ceremony was to be done with great solemnity so that the priests themselves might be duly affected with the greatness of the work they were called to, and so that the people might learn to magnify the office and none dare invade it. What was being done, on his account, was that men whom God had chosen gave themselves up to his service and God declared his acceptance of them — so that everyone knew they had not glorified themselves to be made priests but were called of God. He draws the general rule from it: all who are to be employed for God are to be sanctified to him, the person accepted first and the performance afterwards.

The Hebrew idiom for consecrating catches Henry's attention, and he works it hard. To consecrate is to fill the hand, and the ram of consecration is the ram of fillings; he thinks the phrase probably borrowed from the putting of the sacrifice into the priest's hand to be waved. From it he takes two things about ministers. Their hands are full, so that they have no time to trifle, the work being great and copious and constant. And their hands must be filled — of necessity they must have something to offer, they cannot find it in themselves, and it must be given them from above; they cannot fill the people's hearts unless God fills their hands.

Henry also notices who performed the rite and where. Moses did it, by God's appointment: though a priest is ordained for men, the people were not to consecrate him, and Moses as the Lord's servant and agent did the priest's work for this once, which is why the priest's portion of the sacrifice is here assigned to him. The place was the door of the tabernacle, and Henry finds that fitting rather than incidental — those who were to mediate between God and man, standing between both, were consecrated at the door because they were to be doorkeepers.

Calvin declines to say much here, promising a fuller treatment when the same material returns in Leviticus, and adds that it is not his custom to invent mysteries out of vague speculations that would gratify readers rather than instruct them. What he does say is compressed into a single line of argument. Because the whole human race is corrupt and infected with many impurities, so that a man's uncleanness bars his access to God, Moses washes the priests before consecrating them; from which Calvin gathers that the true purity which was only typical under the law is found in Christ alone, the high priest who became us being holy, harmless, undefiled and separate from sinners.
2:
The provisions are listed before the ceremony, and Ellicott explains why. The first thing to be done was to prepare the victims that would be needed and have them ready against the time of sacrifice; the requirement that they be without blemish he renders more strictly as perfect. On the bread he supplies a reason the text withholds: nothing leavened was allowed, fermentation being regarded as a species of corruption and so a bar to purity.

Clarke counts three sorts and separates them by shape rather than ingredient, since none had leaven in it — the plain kind, whatever its outline; the pricked or perforated cake, so named from its root; and a third whose root means to be attenuated, an exceedingly slender biscuit which he thinks the English properly renders wafer. Ellicott describes them by their handling instead: a tolerably thick cake over which oil has been poured, and beside it something extremely slight and unsubstantial, as its etymology implies, oil being eaten with either.

The two ways of applying the oil are separated as carefully as the shapes: one batch has it poured or mingled over, the second is anointed with it, so the difference lies in preparation and not in what the eater does afterwards. Clarke keeps the Hebrew before him throughout, and it is his reliance on the roots — perforate, attenuate — that lets him sort by form where the English translation blurs them together.

Gill and Keil and Delitzsch add only what the text says about the material and the carriage — that all of them were to be made of wheaten flour, and that the whole was to be put into a single basket and brought in the basket along with the bullock and the two rams. It is a small detail, and none of the commentators makes anything of it; but it is the one point at which the chapter shows the offerings being carried rather than described, and it fixes the moment when the ceremony proper is about to begin, with the animals led and the basket in hand at the door of the tent.
4:
The washing is the first act, and Ellicott stops on it longer than on anything else in the ceremony. This is the first mention in Scripture of a religious ablution, and he treats the fact as unremarkable rather than striking: water is so natural a symbol of purity, and washing so apt a representation of the purging of sin, that its wide use across religions of very different characters is no surprise. He lists them — Egypt, Persia, Greece, Italy — and then meets the objection they might seem to raise. Their employment of the symbol was no argument against its adoption here, since the legislation of Sinai was not meant to annul or supersede natural religion but to improve and expand it; and since the same symbolism kept its place in the ceremonial of Christianity, it was suitable a fortiori for the earlier and less spiritual dispensation. He also fixes the place from what comes later: the laver, not yet mentioned but already designed, stood between the brazen altar and the tent, and rabbinical tradition puts it not directly opposite the door but a little toward the south.

Clarke and Wesley read the washing plainly, as signifying that those who bear the vessels of the Lord must be clean and must put away all filthiness of flesh and spirit. Wesley then carries the sequence forward and gives each act its meaning as it comes: they were clothed because it is not enough to put away the pollutions of sin, the graces of the Spirit must also be put on; they were girded as men prepared and strengthened for their work; they were robed and crowned as men who counted their office their true honour.

On the investiture Ellicott is the most exact. The garments are those described in the previous chapter, the linen tunic being the innermost and so put on first; and from the fuller account in Leviticus he counts nine distinct acts, from the tunic and its girdle through the robe, the ephod and its girdle, the breastplate with the Urim and Thummim placed in its bag, to the mitre and the golden plate fastened to its front. Directions this minute, he adds, may fairly be held to justify the equally minute ones given in the English Ordinal for the vesting of bishops at their consecration. Clarke explains the vocabulary instead, deriving the word invest from the clothing itself, since a man appointed to an office and habited for it was said to be invested with it. Gill reads one detail of the robing for its moral: Aaron was girded with the girdle of the ephod and his sons with common girdles made for them, all of which showed what strength, diligence and expedition their office would require.

The anointing draws Clarke's longest note in this part of the chapter. Anointing with oil marked the communication of the gifts and graces of the Spirit, and was used at the installation of prophets, priests and kings — the prophet because no man can foretell events unless inspired, the priest because none can offer acceptable sacrifice or minister profitably in holy things unless enlightened and directed, the king because no man can frame just laws or use power only against vice unless he is under the inspiration of the Almighty. From there Clarke reaches his point: no man ever held all three offices, and so no man but Jesus ever bore the title of the Anointed One, of whom Melchizedek and Aaron and David were types without ever having the name. Ellicott gives the same emblem more briefly, and finds in the pouring of the oil on the head a sign of the freeness and abundance with which God gives grace to his servants; Wesley adds that the church might thereby be filled with the sweet savour of his administrations.
10:
Why a sin offering has to come first is what Wesley fastens on. The law made men priests who had infirmity, so they must offer for their own sin before they could make atonement for anyone else's. The laying on of hands he reads as a confession — the offerers acknowledging that they deserved to die for their own sin and desiring that the killing of the beast be accepted as a vicarious satisfaction in their place.

Clarke describes the same gesture as a rite with two effects at once: it consecrated the animal to God, making it proper to be offered, and it signified that the offerer was giving up the life of the beast as an atonement to redeem his own life from the death his sinfulness had deserved. He reports the form the act later took, the hands laid between the horns and the sin confessed over the victim — I have sinned, I have done iniquity, and do return by repentance before thee, and with this I make atonement — after which the animal was reckoned to bear the offerer's sins vicariously. Ellicott puts the transaction more starkly still. By this symbolical action, commanded in every sin offering, the offerer identified himself with the animal and transferred his guilt to it; the animal thereby became accursed, its death paid the penalty due to the sins laid upon it, and those who had committed them went free — as Christ, he adds, was made a curse for us.

The handling of the blood follows a fixed pattern, and Ellicott states it as a rule rather than an instance. In every sin offering some of the blood was smeared on the horns of the altar and the remainder poured out at its base; the virtue of the altar was held to reside especially in its horns, which is why fugitives in the later histories clung to them.

What was burnt on the altar and what was burnt elsewhere is the point of the closing verses, and here Ellicott is unusually informative about ancient practice generally. Whole burnt offerings were comparatively rare in the old world; usually only parts of a victim went up in fire, the greater portion being eaten by priests and worshippers or burnt away from the altar. Among the parts thought most fitting for the altar the fat always held a high place, which he accounts for either by its being reckoned a delicacy or by the readiness with which it caught and burned in a clear bright blaze. Gill identifies the membranes precisely, and Ellicott names the one above the liver as what is sometimes called the little omentum.

The remainder went outside the camp, and all three commentators agree on why. Ellicott gives the general rule for sin offerings: the whole animal was reckoned too impure for any part of it to be fit for human food. Wesley draws the contrast that matters to him — the flesh of other sin offerings was eaten by the priests, in token of the priests taking away the people's sin, but this one was burnt outside the camp to signify the imperfection of the legal dispensation, since the sins of the priests themselves could not be taken away by such sacrifices, and a better high priest with a better sacrifice had to be looked for. Gill reads the same burning as representing a whole Christ under all his sufferings and the shame and reproach he underwent in them.
15:
Wesley states the logic of the order before the animal is described: the sin offering had to come first and the burnt offering after, since until guilt is removed no acceptable service can be performed. The ram wholly burnt he reads as the dedication of the men themselves wholly to God, living sacrifices kindled with fire and ascending in the flame of holy love. Clarke marks it simply as a burnt offering and refers the class back to his fuller treatment elsewhere. Ellicott makes the difference from the first victim the point. A burnt offering represented self-sacrifice and was therefore entirely acceptable, so that the whole might be consumed on the altar, where of a sin offering only certain parts could be. Gill notes the practical consequence in the arranging: the head, the pieces, the inwards and the legs were all laid in order together on the altar because the whole was to go up.

Over the handling of the blood Ellicott corrects the English. The word here is not the one properly rendered sprinkle, which comes three verses later, but one meaning rather to scatter or throw — the act intended is casting the blood from a basin against the lower part of the altar. He adds how it was managed in practice, by throwing it on two corners, the north-east and the south-west, which moistened all four sides at once.

The phrase about a sweet savour Ellicott is careful to keep from being read grossly. It was a general heathen notion that the gods were actually delighted by the odour of sacrifices, and he sees no just ground for taxing the Hebrews with anything so coarse and materialistic: the expression here, as in Genesis and repeatedly in Leviticus and Numbers, is metaphorical.

Calvin, treating the whole consecration together, states the principle the blood-rites rest on. The priest must be sprinkled with blood in order that he may conciliate God's favour toward himself for the purpose of intercession — and so, he says, the priesthood of Christ was itself dedicated with blood, that it might be efficacious to reconcile God with us. He then raises the objection his own reading invites and answers it: since only the right ear and the right thumb and toe were smeared, were the priests consecrated in half their persons only? His reply is that in the one part the other is comprehended, both ears and both hands and feet having the same office, so that what is said of one holds of the other.

Why those members and not others he treats as the more interesting question. He does not doubt that the ear designates obedience and the hands and feet the actions and the whole course of a life, since Scripture constantly uses cleanness of hands for integrity of living and a way or walk for the manner of it. It is fitting, then, that a man's life should be consecrated by blood; and because obedience is the foundation of well-doing and is preferred to all sacrifices, Moses is told to begin at the ear. If anyone objects that the tongue matters no less, the priest being the messenger of the Lord of hosts, Calvin answers that the office of teaching is not in view here but only that of intercession, and that in these three members everything belonging to atonement was embraced. His last qualification is about the antitype rather than the type: what is said of Christ's consecration does not apply to his own person, since he was not anointed for his own sake nor needed to borrow grace from blood, but had regard to his members and devoted himself wholly to their salvation.
19:
The third animal is the strange one, and every commentator says so. Ellicott calls it by far the most peculiar part of the whole ceremony: consecrated to God by sacrifice, its blood served with the holy oil to consecrate Aaron and his sons, while its most sacred parts were laid on their hands so that they might perform their first priestly act with them — which he reckons not merely the crowning act of the rite but its most essential feature, the one that imparted the priestly character. Clarke explains the name from the same practice. It is the ram of filling up, because a man being dedicated had his hands filled with an offering proper to the occasion, and the filling of the hands signified that he now had a right to offer sacrifice. He carries the custom sideways into two other spheres: in the East every inferior brought a present when admitted to a superior's presence, so the sacrifice was at once atonement and gift; and in the English church a Bible is put into a priest's hands at his ordination with words giving him authority to preach, which Clarke takes to be in reference to this ancient mode.

Wesley classes it a peace offering and finds the comfort of the priesthood in it, where the burnt offering had yielded God the glory. Dividing the blood between God and the men he takes for a token of mutual covenant, part flung against the altar and part laid on their persons and garments, so that the expiation was at once applied and assured and the men themselves sanctified throughout. Its going to the extremities he reads as deliberate: neither the tip of the ear nor the great toe excepted, the whole man enclosed and taken in for God. And the flesh divided the same way, so that, he says with reverence, God and they might feast together in token of friendship and fellowship.

On the three members themselves the readings converge without quite repeating one another. Clarke takes the rite to dedicate every faculty — the ear to hearing and studying the law, the hand to diligence in the ministry and every act of obedience, the foot to walking in the way of God's precepts — and draws the sharper inference that no priest could hear, work or walk acceptably unless the sacrifice were first applied to him. Ellicott begins instead from what blood was held to be. It was the life; the life consecrated to God and accepted by him was given back to his ministers so as to consecrate them wholly, and so placed on the ear it reminded them to keep it open to the divine voice, on the thumb that they should take nothing in hand but what was sanctified, on the toe that they were to walk thenceforth in the paths of holiness.

The sprinkling that follows is twofold, and Ellicott reads the pairing closely: blood and oil together denoted a twofold holiness, justification by the atoning blood and sanctification by the outpouring of the Spirit. He notes too that this seems to have been the only anointing Aaron's sons received. Gill is careful about the mechanics — the blood taken was not what had been thrown against the altar, which could not have been gathered up again, but what stood in the basin on it.
22:
The parts set aside are the ones usually burnt in a peace offering, and both Ellicott and Clarke stop on one of them. What the English calls the rump is the broad fat tail of the Oriental sheep, which Ellicott reports at between six and twenty pounds. Clarke has heard higher figures still, from twelve to forty, and quotes Ludolf's account of what the weight obliges: the owners tie a little cart behind the animal and lay the tail on it, partly for convenience of carriage and to ease the creature, partly to keep the wool out of the dirt and the tail from being torn among bushes and stones. It is the one point in this chapter where a commentator supplies a picture rather than a doctrine.

The waving itself Ellicott describes with unusual physical precision, and would correct the preposition to do it. The offerings were placed on the hands of Aaron and his sons; Moses then put his own hands beneath theirs and made the waving motion toward the four quarters of the sky, presenting the offerings to a God who is everywhere. What follows from that arrangement is his real point: Aaron and his sons performed their first priestly act as passive instruments in Moses' hands, moved by his muscular energy, and by these means their priestly character was made complete.

Clarke reads the same moment as a question of standing rather than of motion. Aaron and his sons are here still merely private persons bringing an offering, without authority to present it themselves except through a priest; Moses was to them at this point what they would afterwards be to Israel. Gill takes the filled hands forward into the antitype — all things relative to the glory of God and the good of his people are in Christ's hands, and since he too must have somewhat to offer, his hands are filled and he has a sufficiency for the purpose. Wesley describes the sequence plainly: the parts were first waved in token of being offered to God and then burnt, the altar devouring God's portion, so that God admitted Aaron and his sons to wait at his table and took the meat of his altar from their hands. Ellicott adds that Moses was not to lay his borrowed priestly function down immediately, but having begun the ceremony was to complete it.

The two gestures that name these portions draw Clarke's most speculative note. The wave offering was moved to and fro, right and left; the heave offering lifted up and let down, and this several times. He reports Houbigant's conjecture — carefully, and with an apology for its boldness — that the twofold action traced the figure of the cross, on which the great peace offering between God and man was lifted up, prefigured by all the ancient victims. Clarke will not assert it, saying only that had we authority for the conjecture it would cast much light, and that Houbigant's judgment earns it a respectful hearing. What he does assert is the practical outcome, that breast and shoulder became the priests' portion for ever; and he notes with some relish that Moses, never consecrated to the priesthood himself, here acts as high priest, consecrates one, and takes the priest's portion — being an extraordinary messenger whose authority came immediately from God, much as Christ gave his apostles authority to baptize without evidence of having baptized them.
26:
Why the two portions in particular is a question Gill answers from the high priest's dress. The shoulder was his because Aaron bore the names of the tribes on his shoulders for a memorial, and the breast for the same reason, because he bore their names in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart and their judgment before the Lord continually. He notes that the arrangement was an everlasting statute only in the sense the priesthood was — binding as long as Aaron's order lasted, and ended when the Messiah came.

Ellicott accounts for Moses receiving the breast by the general law of wave offerings, which gave it to the officiating priest — and Moses was officiating. Wesley reads the eating that follows as the warmest thing in the chapter: Aaron and his sons ate the flesh and the bread at the door of the tent, which signified that God called them not servants only but friends, so that he supped with them and they with him; and their eating the very things by which atonement was made signified their thankful acceptance of its benefit and their joyful communion with God upon it.

Calvin turns to the restrictions and reads them all as guarding one thing. Strangers are forbidden the holy portions lest the dignity of offerings called the holiness of the Lord be impaired: if anyone might touch and eat them there would be no distinction between them and ordinary food. He notes that some of the priest's portions were common to all his household while the holy parts were excepted, so that this particular instance might teach the reverence due to the whole. The rule about place he explains the same way, since eating what was holy inside their own houses would have blurred the same line; and the burning of what remained he reads as a precaution against indignity rather than against uncleanness — if the flesh grew rank or the bread mouldy, the ill savour and filthy appearance would detract from the dignity of holy things. All of it, he says, was childish rudiment suited to the infirmity of that people, and all of it had one object, that no corruption should creep in to pollute the service of God or render it contemptible.

The succession is settled briefly. Gill records the Targum's gloss that the son who rises in his stead must be of Aaron's own family and not merely of the tribe of Levi, descending through Eleazar or Ithamar.

The seven days give Clarke his opening for a long excursus on the number itself. Seven is the Hebrew number of perfection, often used for the completion or fullness of a thing, since it holds the whole course of the days in which the world was made and the rest appointed; a consecration lasting seven days therefore signified a perfect consecration, and told the priest that his whole body and soul, his time and his talents, were devoted to God and the people. Clarke then traces the idea outward. He reports the Essene explanation preserved by Philo and Josephus, that seven is sacred because it results from the side of a square added to those of a triangle, admits the formula conveys nothing as it stands, and unpacks it from the Pythagoreans. The triangle, having beginning, middle and end, was the emblem of wisdom and, being the shape of the wedge and incapable of destruction, the emblem of spirit; the square stood for solid matter. Seven, holding both, becomes an emblem of body and spirit together, comprehending the intellectual and the natural world at once — which is perhaps what Cicero meant in calling seven the knot and cement of all things. Clarke offers the chain of transmission with it, from the Hebrews to the Egyptians to the Greeks, and ends by leaving the ancient philosophers to be the best judges of their own meaning.
35:
Why the ceremony had to last a week is answered pastorally by Wesley and structurally by Ellicott. Wesley grants that all the ceremonies were performed on the first day, but the consecration was not to be reckoned complete until the seventh — which put a solemnity on the admission, set a distance between this state and the former one, and obliged the men to enter their work with a pause long enough to consider its weight. He notes the practice continued: a successor to the high priesthood was to wear the holy garments seven days together, so that one sabbath at least should pass over him in his consecration. Ellicott takes the number as the one used almost exclusively under the old covenant wherever acts reach their result by repetition, and reads the command here as a sevenfold repetition of the entire ceremonial.

The daily sin offering troubles Wesley in the way it is meant to. Repeating it every day of the seven intimated that though atonement was made they must still keep up a penitent sense of sin and often repeat the confession of it; and beyond that, that sacrifices offered day by day could not perfect those who came by them, since otherwise they would have ceased to be offered — so that a better hope had to be looked for. Gill reads the sevenfold repetition the same way, as figuring by that number the full expiation which these offerings could not themselves obtain.

Wesley then sets the whole rite against its antitype point by point: a high priest called of God and consecrated for evermore, anointed with the Spirit above his fellows, clothed with glory and beauty for holy garments, and sanctified by his own blood rather than that of bullocks and rams. Believers he makes spiritual priests on the same pattern, washed in that blood, clothed with the beauty of holiness, having received the anointing; and where Moses put blood on Aaron with his finger, Wesley sees the Spirit — called the finger of God — applying the merit of Christ to the conscience. His last inference is about ordination now: gospel ministers are to be set apart with the same deliberation and seriousness, in the ordainers as much as in the ordained.

The altar is consecrated alongside the men, and that raises Calvin's difficulty. Since the altar was no less a type of Christ than the priest, what can its cleansing mean, as though there were something impure in Christ? His answer is the rule he has used before, that no similitude is identical with the reality — otherwise the shadows could not be shadows. The likeness still holds where it matters: it shows that God could be propitiated toward the human race only by an expiation made with blood, so the altar had not merely to be cleansed but dedicated, that reconciliation might proceed from it. Ellicott would render the clause by making an atonement rather than when, and identifies the act with the smearing of blood on the horns.

The closing phrase is read two ways. Calvin notes that some take it in the masculine — whoever touches it shall be holy, understood of the priest — but prefers to read it of the offerings, so that the altar's consecration is dignified by its consequence, sanctifying the victims laid on it; the sum being that Christ's body, offered and consecrated with blood, was acceptable to God, and its holiness blots out our uncleanness. Clarke reads it as property rather than person: whatever was laid on the altar became the Lord's and had to be wholly devoted to sacred uses. Ellicott turns the grammar round altogether and makes it a prohibition — must be holy, nothing unholy may touch it, the future carrying the force of an imperative as it does in the commandments.
38:
Henry states what the daily service secured. Whatever else might or might not be offered on a given day, these two lambs were sure to be offered, at the public charge, for the benefit of all Israel — to make atonement for their daily sins and to acknowledge their daily mercies. Calvin gives the arrangement first place among all the sacrifices for the same reason, and explains why a daily one was needed alongside the yearly entry into the holiest: the people had to have another kind of victim set before their eyes every day, so that they might reflect that they stood in constant need of being reconciled, and so learn from morning to evening to fly to God's mercy.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the quantities and are candid about how uncertain they are. A tenth of fine flour and a quarter of a hin of beaten oil to each lamb, with a quarter of a hin of wine for a drink offering — but the tenth is the tenth of an ephah, which Bertheau reckons at nearly two hundred Parisian cubic inches while Thenius sets it at about half that, and the Rabbins at forty-three hen's eggs of average size. The hin they measure the same way and with the same spread, so that a quarter of it comes to eighteen eggs.

Calvin will not let the oil and wine be read as flavouring. God was not gratified by their sweet savour, nor did he wish to accustom the priests to delicacies and make them epicures under colour of religion, since the scent of wine cannot in itself please God. The seasonings were there so that the people should not rest in bare and empty figures but acknowledge something better underlying them — the savour meaning nothing else than the spiritual truth, that they should bring faith and repentance to the sacrifice. He notes that heathen nations partly imitated the rite, and quotes Horace on refusing cakes like a runaway from the priests to show that cakes were offered to idols everywhere; but that, he says, was blind mimicry, men supposing their gods took pleasure like human beings in sweet and delicate foods.

The word continual Calvin takes with a qualification that comes from prophecy rather than from Exodus. It was called continual because God commanded it through all generations, but Daniel shows it was temporary, ceasing at the coming of Christ — and from that he gathers that this sacrifice was directing the people's minds to Christ all along. What the ancients had by way of figure now returns as profit to us: since Christ was offered once and by that one offering consecrated us for ever, the daily sacrifice under the law teaches that by the benefit of his death pardon is always ready.

Clarke supplies the long afterlife of the ordinance, these two being generally called the morning and evening daily sacrifices and offered from the settlement in the promised land until the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, with the Jewish account of their use attached. Wesley reaches the same conclusion by the shorter road. The lamb morning and evening typified the continual intercession Christ lives to make in the virtue of his satisfaction, so that one offering made once for all becomes a continual offering; and the practical lesson he draws is that we are to offer the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise every day, morning and evening, acknowledging our dependence. Gill puts the same terminus more plainly still, the offering standing as long as the Mosaic economy lasted, until he came who ended it by offering up himself.
43:
Calvin uses the closing promise to settle what the tabernacle's name means, and does it by philology rather than assertion. Translators have made the word testimony, or church, or assembly, or appointment; but Moses gives the reason for the name in the same breath, using the verb the noun derives from, and that verb means to contract or agree with another, or at least to meet for the transaction of business. So the tabernacle of the convention is the place God chose and appointed for his people, where he and they might come together. Calvin notes an alternative derivation from a root meaning to protest by solemn rite, and sets it aside as against grammar.

What follows from the name is the point. That God invited his people to familiar colloquy was, on Calvin's reading, of the greatest weight in preserving a modest reverence toward the priests; and the repetition in the next verse lays down a law for all Israel, that whoever wishes to be counted among them must not turn aside or wander elsewhere but seek God there. The place is to be sanctified because God will magnificently display his glory in it — and God's whole design, Calvin concludes, was to keep the people bound to him by the tie of the Levitical priesthood.

One qualification he presses hard, and it is the one the passage itself makes. It is God alone who sanctifies — the place, the offerings and the men alike. From that he turns on those who claim more than God has conferred: the Pope, in whom holiness itself is said to reside, produces no divine authority for the title but vaunts himself on inventions, and the claim of priests to offer Christ meets the same question, by what authority, since God reserves to himself the right of sanctifying those who exercise a lawful priesthood. The positive doctrine Calvin takes from the same verses is that Christ is not to be estimated humanly but according to his heavenly and divine power.

Clarke and Ellicott read the promise of sanctifying as reaching past the ceremony just described. Clarke infers that the consecration Moses performed was only symbolical, and that Aaron and his sons had to be made holy by God himself before they could officiate — from which he draws the wider rule that no designation by man is sufficient to qualify anyone for holy things. Ellicott says the same and extends it in time: something beyond the formal consecration is intended, God continually sanctifying that priesthood by the presence of his Spirit in their ministerial acts and even in their daily walk, if they seek to serve him. On the indwelling itself Ellicott warns against reducing the promise to the presence of the cloud in the tent, since it pledged God to a perpetual supervision and tender protection such as the nation's history actually shows; and Clarke calls it the great charter of God's people under both Testaments. The knowing at the end both take as acknowledgment rather than information — Clarke noting that the word often bears that sense in Scripture, and Ellicott that God's after-care would prove him the same God whose help had brought them out of Egypt. Gill fills in what the dwelling amounted to in practice: God took up residence in the tent set in the middle of the camp, like a king in his palace, near at hand to help and defend his subjects and supply what they needed; and the knowing he grounds in the same experience, in God's presence with them, the blessings bestowed, the care taken and the kindness shown. What the chapter began with, the filling of a man's hands, it ends by referring back to the one who fills them; and the promise of indwelling, rather than the consecration of any priest, is what the whole ceremony has been arranged to secure.
